title: SYSK Selects: How Panic Attacks Work
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of a 2014 episode on panic attacks and panic disorder. The hosts cover the symptoms (the DSM list, where four or more symptoms signal a panic attack), how panic disorder is diagnosed, and how it differs from a heart attack. They explain the autonomic nervous system and the fight, flight or freeze response, and discuss a reported gene (NKRT3), genetic versus environmental causes, serotonin and GABA, and agoraphobia. Treatments covered are SSRIs, benzodiazepines, beta blockers and CBT with exposure therapy, along with diaphragmatic breathing and coping tips. The episode closes with a listener mail about basement fear and an outro.

segments.title: Opening and Widespread Panic aside
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode as a Saturday Select pick about panic attacks. The hosts briefly discuss a concert attack at a Widespread Panic show, then set the topic apart from psychotic breaks.

segments.title: Panic disorder prevalence and fight, flight or freeze
segments.summary: The hosts say about 2.8 percent of Americans have panic disorder, and that panic attacks can occur once without a disorder. They explain the fight, flight or freeze response and how a panic attack involves fear with no real danger present.

segments.title: Symptoms and diagnosis
segments.summary: The hosts list the DSM symptoms, of which four or more suggest a panic attack. Panic disorder is diagnosed after four attacks within four weeks, or one attack followed by a month of fear of another.

segments.title: Autonomic nervous system and the adrenaline response
segments.summary: The hosts explain the autonomic nervous system and its sympathetic and parasympathetic parts. Adrenaline drives the panic response, and the calming parasympathetic response fails to kick in during a panic attack.

segments.title: Causes: genes, childhood trauma and brain chemistry
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the reported NKRT3 gene, identical versus fraternal twin studies, childhood trauma, an overactive fear system, and the roles of serotonin and GABA. They also cover demographics, with panic disorder twice as common in women and typically starting in the twenties.

segments.title: Agoraphobia, phobias and the evolutionary theory
segments.summary: The hosts describe how fear of a place where a panic attack happened can lead to agoraphobia and phobias. They recall Freudian explanations and dismiss a 1980s evolutionary argument about women and panic disorder as bunk. They also discuss how families may over- or underreact.

segments.title: Treatments: SSRIs, anti-anxiety drugs and beta blockers
segments.summary: The hosts say panic disorder is highly treatable, with success rates of about 60 to 90 percent through medication and therapy. They cover SSRIs, which take two to four weeks to work, benzodiazepines such as Xanax with dependency risks, and beta blockers, including Chuck's personal experience.

segments.title: Cognitive behavioral therapy and exposure therapy
segments.summary: The hosts describe CBT for panic disorder: education, self-monitoring, breathing practice, and gradual exposure to feared situations such as elevators. They also cover acknowledging panic attacks, the coping challenge of recurrence, and a comparison to LSD trips.

segments.title: Breathing techniques, helping others and lifestyle
segments.summary: The hosts explain diaphragmatic breathing with exercises that use pillows and a book on the stomach. They advise how to help someone having a panic attack, recommend exercise and mindfulness, and suggest cutting caffeine, sugar and nicotine.
topics: helping someone during a panic attack

segments.title: Personal stories and panic attack versus heart attack
segments.summary: Josh describes a college roommate's panic attack during finals and his wife Emily's panic attack while driving. The hosts then list heart attack warning signs from the American Heart Association and advise calling for help when in doubt.

segments.title: Listener mail: basement fear
segments.summary: A listener named Kelsey from Kansas City, Kansas, says she uses Stuff You Should Know episodes to calm irrational basement fear during wedding-planning stress, which the hosts link to exposure therapy.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts give contact information and sign off.
